Here is the verse-by-verse commentary on Joshua 6, drawing from the sources retrieved.

---

## Joshua 6 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1 — Jericho Tightly Shut

**Traditional reading:** This verse functions as a parenthesis, describing the state of Jericho while Joshua was receiving instructions from the Commander of the LORD’s army (Joshua 5:13–15). The Hebrew repeats the verb *cagar* ("shut") twice for emphasis — "shutting and was shut" — underscoring that the city was sealed with extreme vigilance, both from within (iron doors, brazen bars, according to the Targum) and blockaded from without by Israel. The verse highlights the seemingly impossible obstacle facing Israel, an army unskilled in siege warfare, so that the coming miracle would stand out all the more clearly. Matthew Henry adds that Jericho "resolves Israel shall not be its master … thus were they foolish, and their hearts hardened to their destruction."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-6-commentary (Precept Austin, citing Woudstra, Enns, Matthew Henry)

---

### v. 2 — "I Have Delivered Jericho into Your Hand"

**Traditional reading:** The speaker is the same divine Person from Joshua 5:14 — the Captain of the LORD’s host. God speaks in the past tense ("I have given"), signalling that what He purposes is as good as done. Despite Jericho’s fierce warriors and fortified walls, the LORD promises a certain and easy victory. Gill notes that the fear already fallen on the inhabitants and their self-imposed lockdown was evidence that God had already handed them over.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/ (Guzik)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)

**Reformed/Baptist (Piper/Desiring God):** John Piper emphasises that Jericho’s fall illustrates that "God was her commander-in-chief. He gave all the orders, and he himself fought for them" — the conquest was not Israel’s own doing but God’s.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-conquest-of-canaan

---

### vv. 3–5 — The Battle Plan

**Traditional reading:** God’s plan made no military sense — no siege engines, no assault, no undermining of walls. Instead, a daily silent procession: armed men, seven priests with seven ram’s-horn trumpets before the ark, and a rear guard. For six days, once around the city. On the seventh day, seven circuits, a long trumpet blast, the people’s shout, and the walls would collapse "under themselves." The number seven appears 14 times in the chapter, symbolising totality, completion, and the covenant seal between God and Israel (Keil, Hengstenberg). The design was to impress the Canaanites with divine omnipotence, to teach Israel faith, and to exalt the ark as the symbol of God’s presence.

Gill, citing Kimchi, reports a Jewish tradition that the wall was "swallowed up in its place under the earth, and a little of it appear above ground for a memorial of the miracle." Guzik notes that the approximately half-mile walk around the 7-acre city required active participation from Israel — God did not act while they stood aside.

On the trumpets: "rams' horns" translates Hebrew *yobel*, the same root as "jubilee." Gill, citing R. Akiba, says Arabs called a ram *jobel*, and the trumpet was named after the ram’s horn. JFB notes the horns were probably literal animal horns at first, with the name preserved even when metal trumpets were later used.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/ (Guzik)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-6-commentary (Precept Austin)

### vv. 6–7 — Joshua’s Prompt Obedience

**Traditional reading:** Joshua immediately and unreservedly communicated God’s unusual orders to the priests and people. Trapp (cited by Guzik) praises his "prompt and present obedience, ready and speedy, without shucking or hucking, without delays and consults." JFB says Joshua "surrendered all his own views, at once and unreservedly, to the declared will of God." Gill specifies that Joshua called the priests (not ordinary Levites or Kohathites) for this special task. The armed men were to go before the ark to guard it, protect the priests, and defend against any sally from the city.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/ (Guzik, citing Trapp)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)

---

### vv. 8–14 — The March of Six Days

**Traditional reading:** The procession order: armed men first, then seven trumpet-blowing priests, then the ark (carried by priests), then the rear guard. The ark is mentioned 11 times in the chapter (Redpath, cited by Guzik) — the central feature. The people were commanded to utter not a single word during the six days (v. 10). This profound silence, broken only by the short trumpet blasts, tested Israel’s faith profoundly. They saw the impressive walls daily and had to trust God without immediate results. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "Faith is not a fool, faith does not shut her eyes to difficulty … Faith sees the difficulty, surveys it all, and then she says, ‘By my God will I leap over a wall.’" JFB quotes Bishop Hall: "Doubtless the people of Jericho made themselves merry with the spectacle."

Gill notes the camp was at Gilgal (Joshua 5:10). Guzik suggests the six days of silence may also have been an expression of God’s grace, giving Jericho "one last opportunity to repent" (Madvig).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/ (Guzik, citing Redpath, Spurgeon, Madvig)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB, citing Bishop Hall)

---

### vv. 15–16 — The Seventh Day

**Traditional reading:** Jewish tradition (cited by Jarchi, Kimchi, and Gill) holds that the seventh day was a Sabbath. Gill quotes Kimchi: "though they slew and burnt on the sabbath day, he that commanded the sabbath commanded to profane the sabbath in the subduing of Jericho." Guzik notes this is a reversal of the creation order: God worked six days and rested on the seventh; here Israel’s most strenuous work fell on the seventh day, as God completed His work of judgment. They rose at dawn because they had seven circuits to complete. At the seventh circuit, Joshua commanded the shout: "for the LORD has given you the city." The shout was both a war cry and an exclamation of praise (Howard, cited by Guzik). JFB notes that this delay "brought out their faith and obedience in so remarkable a manner, that it is celebrated by the apostle (Heb 11:30)."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/ (Guzik)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)

---

### vv. 17–19 — The *Cherem* (Ban) and the Exception of Rahab

**Traditional reading:** The city was placed under *cherem* — devoted to the LORD for utter destruction. JFB explains: when such a ban was pronounced, men and animals were killed, no booty taken, idols burned, and everything either destroyed or consecrated to the sanctuary (cf. Lev 27:28; Deut 7:2; 20:17; 1 Sam 15:3). Jericho, as the firstfruits of the conquest, belonged entirely to the LORD. The severity was justified because the Canaanites had "filled up their iniquities," had resisted the light of the Jordan miracle, and Jericho seems to have been reinforced from all the country (Josh 24:11). Its destruction would "paralyze all the rest of the devoted people."

Rahab alone was excepted "because she hid the messengers." Guzik notes that all Jericho heard about God, but only Rahab responded in faith.

All silver, gold, bronze, and iron were "holy to the LORD" and destined for His treasury. Guzik explains that metals survive fire and were set apart as firstfruits for the sanctuary. The warning against taking any devoted thing (v. 18) foreshadows Achan’s sin in chapter 7.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/ (Guzik, citing Madvig, Hess)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)

**Reformed/Baptist (Piper):** Piper treats the *cherem* command as God’s severe but just judgment. He calls Jericho a city of "honeyed lust" and "brothels," noting that Rahab’s rescue by the scarlet cord is the gospel in miniature — salvation through faith and obedience amidst judgment.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-gospel-of-the-wall-of-jericho

**Baptist (Spurgeon, cited by Guzik):** Spurgeon addressed the moral objection: "Some have dared to speak of it as a hideous massacre; but being commanded of the great Judge, who has the power of life and death, it is to be solemnly regarded as a terrible execution for which there was a stern necessity."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/

---

### vv. 20–21 — The Walls Fall; The City Destroyed

**Traditional reading:** At the long trumpet blast and the people’s great shout, the wall "fell down flat" — a supernatural event that cannot be ascribed to natural causes. Guzik quotes Adam Clarke: "There has been much learned labour spent to prove that the shouting of the people might be the natural cause that the wall fell down! … lost time." The people went "every man straight before him" — because the wall collapsed all around, not in just one place, they could enter directly from every side.

Israel then "devoted to destruction everything in the city — man and woman, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys." JFB comments that "the Canaanites were incorrigible idolaters, addicted to the most horrible vices, and that the righteous judgment of God might sweep them away by the sword … There was mercy mingled with judgment … for while it was directed against one place, time was afforded for others to repent."

Gill sees in Jericho’s fall a type of the fall of mystical Babylon: both are great and wicked; Jericho fell at the sound of ram’s horns (trumpets), Babylon at the seventh angel’s trumpet (Rev 10:7); both never to be rebuilt.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/ (Guzik, citing Clarke, Spurgeon)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)

---

### vv. 22–25 — Rahab Rescued; the City Burned

**Traditional reading:** Joshua remembered the spies' oath (Joshua 2:12–14) and ordered Rahab and all her household brought out. JFB observes that "the town walls were not demolished universally, at least all at once, for Rahab's house was allowed to stand until her relatives were rescued." Rahab's family was placed "outside the camp" — a temporary quarantine, since they were ceremonially unclean Gentiles who needed cleansing from idolatry before full incorporation into Israel (Madvig, cited by Guzik; JFB). Guzik notes that Hebrews 11:31 sets Rahab’s faith in deliberate contrast to the unbelief of Jericho. She "dwells in Israel to this day" — indicating the book was written not long after the events (JFB).

The city was burned with fire; only the precious metals went to the LORD’s treasury.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/ (Guzik, citing Madvig, Hess)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)

---

### v. 26 — Joshua’s Curse on Whoever Rebuilds Jericho

**Traditional reading:** Joshua pronounced a solemn oath (*adjured them*) — a curse binding on Israel and their posterity. The curse declared that anyone who rebuilt Jericho would lose his firstborn at the foundation-laying and his youngest at the setting of the gates (i.e., would become childless during the project). JFB notes this was fulfilled 550 years later in Hiel the Bethelite (1 Kings 16:34). The city’s permanent desolation was designed by God as "a permanent memorial of His abhorrence of idolatry and its attendant vices."

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html (Gill)

---

### v. 27 — The LORD Was with Joshua

**Traditional reading:** The chapter closes with a summary: the LORD’s presence with Joshua was manifest, and his fame spread throughout the land. This is the divine authentication of Joshua’s leadership following the miraculous victory.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/joshua/6.htm (JFB)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/ (Guzik)

## Points of Denominational Distinctiveness

### Reformed / Baptist — Faith as the Instrument

Both Reformed (JFB, Spurgeon) and Baptist (Gill, Piper) traditions stress Hebrews 11:30 ("by faith the walls of Jericho fell") as the interpretive key. The march was an exercise in *faith alone* receiving what God had already promised. Piper emphasises this in his sermon "Future Grace for Finishing the Task," where he groups Jericho’s fall with other miracles that came "by faith." Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) underscores that faith is not blind but "sees the difficulty, surveys it all, and then … leaps over the wall."

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/future-grace-for-finishing-the-task-part-6
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/

### Pentecostal / Charismatic — The Shout and Spiritual Warfare

David Guzik (Enduring Word, from a charismatic tradition) draws application to spiritual warfare: believers "fight from victory, not just for victory." The shout is both war cry and praise — a pattern for Spirit-empowered proclamation. Precept Austin (citing Warren Wiersbe) frames Jericho as a model for "spiritual conflict and victory applicable to our lives today," identifying "three principles of spiritual conflict."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-6/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-6-commentary

### Baptist — Gill’s Typological Reading

Gill (18th-century Baptist) develops an extensive typology: Jericho’s fall prefigures the fall of mystical Babylon (Revelation). The sound of ram’s horns corresponds to gospel preaching; the seven priests at the seventh time on the seventh day correspond to the seventh trumpet and seventh vial. Jericho also pictures the conversion of individual souls: "strong holds of sin and Satan are brought down … by means of the sound of the Gospel."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-6.html

### Modern Scholarship / Archaeological Notes

**Not found from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org** due to search limits. However, Precept Austin includes a note from the NIV Study Bible stating that archaeological excavations at Tell es-Sultan reveal Jericho may have been one of the oldest cities in the world, with settlement from c. 7000 BC, and that by Joshua’s day more than two dozen cities had been built and destroyed on the site. Jericho may have been a centre for moon-god worship (the name perhaps meaning "moon city"). The same source notes the double-wall system: an outer wall 6 ft thick, ~20 ft high; an inner wall ~12 ft thick, ~30 ft high, with a 15 ft walkway between.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-6-commentary
